newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead looks awesome but Dole full of fight.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead looks awesome but Dole full of fight.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole charged into the home-stretch of the Nov. 5 election campaign on Thursday with Clinton looking unbeatable but Dole still full of fight.

As if to show himself undaunted after a final campaign debate in which he clearly failed to land any knockout blow, Dole remained in California to woo voters in a political treasure-trove state where Clinton holds a wide lead.

While many analysts say the 73-year-old Republican is wasting valuable campaign funds by fighting on in places like this, Dole running mate Jack Kemp insisted such pessimism is unwarranted and a historic comeback is in the making.

"That is extremely doable," Kemp said in an ABC Television interview when asked whether the Republican ticket could overcome Clinton leads ranging from high single-digits to near 20 percent with less than three weeks left to Election Day.
Buoyed by his debate performance, Clinton went for a jog on the beach Thursday morning and was making more campaign stops in California later in the day.

Thursday's daily Reuters tracking poll, which traces trends over a three-day average sample among about 900 likely voters, showed Dole moving up slightly to about 12 points behind Clinton in a sampling that did not reflect Wednesday evenings debate performances.
Clinton led Dole in the Reuters/Zogby poll by 45 percent to 33.1 percent with 6.3 percent favouring Reform Party nominee Ross Perot. Dole trailed by about 13 percent on Wednesday.
"These new figures essentially show Clinton dropping, but Dole staying fixed in the low to mid-30s as he has been throughout ... our tracking," said pollster John Zogby.
While other surveys give Clinton slightly bigger or smaller leads, no presidential candidate in modern U.S. history has overcome any such gaps so late in a campaign.

In the celebrated Harry Truman upset of front-runner Thomas Dewey in the 1948 White House race -- a breathtaking comeback often cited by Dole partisans -- Truman only trailed Dewey by about five percentage points in mid-October.

Some Republicans in fact have given up the ghost on Dole and fret about a Clinton rout so vast it might sweep his Democrats back into control of Congress -- which they lost just two years ago -- as well.

The latest Reuters poll, like others suggests a potential for that. About 39 percent of respondents said they would vote for a Democratic candidate for Congress while slightly less than 33 percent said they would back a Republican.
The Democratic lead showed in both houses, although most polls and analysts rate their chances stronger in the House of Representatives than in the Senate.
Kemp and other Dole strategists nonetheless put a positive spin both on the outcome of Wednesday night's second and last Dole-Clinton debate and on the overall campaign prospects.
"The president was playing not to lose," Dole campaign spokesman John Buckley told reporters after the San Diego debate. "But ... Bob Dole connected, sold his economic plan."
Clinton partisans obviously disagreed and they seemed to have the backing of snap post-debate opinion polls, political analysts and ordinary citizens sought out for their views.

An ABC News Poll of 567 registered voters said 55 percent thought Clinton won, 28 percent thought Dole did and 14 percent called it even. As to whether the clash had changed any minds, the pollster said: "What little movement occurred brought Clinton from a 13-point lead among viewers before the debate to a 16-point lead among the same people afterward."

Dole's strategy was to attack Clinton's ethics, credibility and performance in office and he did so at every opportunity while Clinton ignored him and touted his record on a strong U.S. economy, lowering crime rate and other positive news.
"Dole ... inflicted a couple of flesh wounds but Clinton will put on a couple of band-aids and it will be over," said John Pitney, a political scientist at Claremont McKenna College in California.
"It's over unless something happens -- a real blockbuster that suddenly falls from the sky," said Professor Daniel Hallin of the University of California at San Diego.
